content.title: About
content.content: Acorn squash (Cucurbita pepo) is a small winter squash with a ridged, dark green (sometimes orange-streaked) rind, shaped like an acorn, with mildly sweet, nutty, yellow-orange flesh. It originated in the Americas and is usually baked or roasted in halves and stuffed. Acorn squash keeps well for weeks to months after harvest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Acorn squash is named for its acorn-like shape.
It is a winter squash, harvested when mature and with a hard rind.
Its skin is edible when roasted, which makes preparation easy.
It is botanically the same species as zucchini and many pumpkins.
It is often served in halves, stuffed with grains, vegetables, or meat.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Acorn squash contributes fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides potassium, magnesium, and manganese
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure, muscle function, and metabolism.

items.title: Contains carotenoids and B vitamins
items.content: Acorn squash provides carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A, and some B vitamins.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Acorn squash is relatively low in calories for its volume.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Squash allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Acorn squash contains natural sugars and starch, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Potassium considerations
items.content: People with kidney problems or on certain medications should consult a healthcare professional about potassium intake.

items.title: Bitter squash
items.content: Rarely, squash can contain high levels of bitter cucurbitacins that can cause stomach upset. Discard squash that tastes very bitter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Acorn squash can be halved, seeded, and baked or roasted cut-side down, then filled with grains, vegetables, nuts, or sausage, or drizzled with butter, olive oil, or maple syrup. It can also be steamed, microwaved, or pureed into soups. The skin is edible when roasted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole acorn squash in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place for several weeks to a couple of months. Cut squash should be wrapped and refrigerated and used within about five days. Cooked squash can be refrigerated for three to five days or frozen.

chicken-or-turkey-fricassee-with-sauce-n.title: Chicken or Turkey Fricassee with Sauce, No Potatoes (Potatoes Served Separately), Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey fricassee is a tender braised meat dish cooked in a fragrant sauce made from tomatoes, onion, garlic, olive oil, and characteristic Puerto Rican spices: adobo, oregano, cumin, and fresh cilantro. The dish is served without potatoes; potatoes are offered on the side so diners can add them as they wish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican cuisine blends Spanish, African, and Taíno influences, reflected in the bright flavor of fricassee.
The traditional fricassee sauce is simmered slowly, allowing the meat to fully absorb the spice aromas.
The original recipe often includes “pico de gallo,” a fresh salsa of tomatoes, onion, pepper, and lime, served alongside.
Chicken and turkey are frequently marinated in lime juice and olive oil before cooking, making the meat especially juicy.
The dish is commonly accompanied by rice, beans, and fried plantains (tostones) as side dishes.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Skin‑less poultry contains little saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamins B3, B6, and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Adobo, cumin, and fresh cilantro contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Lime juice and garlic boost immunity thanks to vitamin C and sulfur‑rich compounds.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If prepared with pre‑made seasoning mixes, the dish can be high in sodium; salt should be monitored.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Preparing the fricassee alongside seafood or other allergens may lead to cross‑contamination.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Poultry must be cooked to a safe internal temperature to avoid salmonella or campylobacter infection.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fricassee hot, spooning the sauce over the meat. It pairs well with steamed rice, beans, fried plantains, or a fresh salad. Potatoes are served separately—boiled, roasted, or mashed—so each person can add them to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop, adding a splash of broth or water to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice pudding is a classic dessert made from cooked rice, milk, sugar, and flavorings such as vanilla, cinnamon, or raisins. It has a smooth, creamy texture and a mildly sweet taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice pudding is known worldwide: in Italy as riso al latte, in Japan as rice porridge desserts, and in Russia as a sweet rice kissel.
Traditionally it was prepared for holidays and fasting days, often using plant‑based milks as a substitute.
Vegan versions replace dairy with coconut, almond, or oat milk, keeping the dish dairy‑free.
Some regional recipes add nuts, dried fruits, or caramelized sugar for extra flavor.
Rice pudding can be served chilled or warm, straight from the pot.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function and participates in protein synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many desserts, rice pudding typically contains little saturated fat.

items.title: Gentle on digestion
items.content: Soft‑cooked rice and creamy texture are easy to digest, making it suitable for children and sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Traditional recipes use milk; people with dairy sensitivities should use plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so portion control is important for diabetics.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Excess sugar increases calories and may contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Risk of spoilage
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth; keep the pudding refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve rice pudding warm or chilled, topped with cinnamon, cocoa powder, nuts, or fresh berries. It works as a breakfast, dessert, or light snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the finished pudding in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave, adding a splash of milk or water to restore its creamy consistency.

slush-frozen-drink-no-sugar-added.title: Slush frozen drink, no sugar added

content.title: About
content.content: Slush is a frozen beverage made from water, natural fruit extracts and flavorings, prepared without added sugar. It has a light, refreshing texture and a vivid taste achieved through concentrated fruit essences.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Slush is often served at summer cafés and festivals as an alternative to carbonated drinks.
The lack of sugar makes it suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.
Flavor can be enhanced with natural sweeteners such as stevia, but the basic version contains none.
The freezing process retains most of the vitamins and antioxidants present in the fruit extracts.
Slush can be made at home using frozen water and flavorings.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Absence of sugar makes the drink low‑calorie, which is convenient for weight management.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Fruit extracts may provide vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: No artificial colors
items.content: Most versions use only natural color derived from fruits.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: Some formulations may contain synthetic flavorings that could trigger sensitivity in certain individuals.

items.title: Cold shock
items.content: Consuming very cold drinks can cause discomfort in teeth or throat for sensitive people.

items.title: Allergy to fruit extracts
items.content: People with known fruit allergies should check the ingredient list before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sugar‑free slush in a glass or cup; you can add a lemon slice or mint for extra freshness. It is best enjoyed slowly, allowing it to melt and release its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen slush in an airtight container in the freezer at –18 °C. Over time ice crystals may form, so slightly thaw before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka and cola is a popular mixed drink made of vodka and cola in proportions to taste. The beverage offers a refreshing flavor, combining the neutral strength of vodka with the sweetness and carbonation of cola.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The “Vodka‑Cola” cocktail became widely known in the 1990s and turned into one of the best‑selling mixed drinks in bars.
There are many variations: sometimes lemon or lime juice, or a dash of bitters is added to enhance the taste.
In Russia and other CIS countries the drink is often colloquially called “Bloody Mary”, although the original Bloody Mary is made with tomato juice.
The combination of vodka and cola is believed to soften the harshness of the spirit thanks to the sweet, fizzy cola.

items.title: Moderate consumption
items.content: In small amounts the cocktail can promote relaxation and improve mood.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar in cola rapidly raises blood glucose, providing a short‑term energy surge.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Cola contains a large amount of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of diabetes.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Vodka is a strong spirit; excessive intake leads to alcohol poisoning and other health issues.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain medicines and reduce their efficacy.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Pour 30–50 ml of vodka into a glass, fill the rest with cola, and stir gently. Optionally garnish with a lemon or lime wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store vodka in a cool, dark place with the bottle tightly sealed. Keep opened cola refrigerated to maintain carbonation.
